paragraphs: Fine-grained image retrieval means finding images from the same narrow category as a query, even when different categories look similar and members of one category vary considerably. A²-Net addresses this recognition problem together with the cost of searching large image collections. It produces compact hash codes intended to support efficient retrieval while retaining connections to meaningful visual attributes.

The network first uses attention to capture visual representations. An encoder-decoder then learns through reconstruction to extract vectors associated with higher-level attributes, without requiring attribute annotations. A feature decorrelation constraint encourages these vectors to carry less redundant information. The final hash codes are generated from the attribute vectors while seeking to preserve the similarities present in the original representations.

The authors report qualitative advantages over competing methods across five fine-grained datasets. Their quantitative results also indicate strong correspondence between the codes and certain important object properties. This connects the retrieval representation to recognizable attributes, rather than treating compactness and visual meaning as unrelated objectives.
neurips-2021-a-2-net-learning-attribute-.tldr: A²-Net learns compact image-retrieval codes that correspond to visual attributes without requiring attribute annotations.

paragraphs: This paper studies construction as a sequence of decisions: an agent must assemble an object from LEGO bricks while obeying connection rules and preventing overlap. The target is supplied through one or more images, rather than a complete description of its volume. The agent therefore has to interpret incomplete visual information while choosing actions that support later construction.

The authors use reinforcement learning because each placement affects the possibilities available afterward. A central challenge is that the action space changes size as construction progresses and contains many invalid placements. Their Brick-by-Brick model includes an action validity prediction network that filters out invalid actions before an actor-critic network chooses how to continue building.

The reported demonstrations show that the method learns to construct an unseen object from a single image or multiple views. The contribution combines reasoning about a visually specified target with sequential planning under geometric constraints. Filtering invalid actions addresses a practical obstacle within that planning process: many available placements would otherwise create overlapping bricks.
neurips-2021-brick-by-brick-combinatoria.tldr: Brick-by-Brick learns to assemble objects from images using reinforcement learning and a network that filters invalid brick placements.

paragraphs: Exemplar variational autoencoders use a prior informed by examples from a dataset, but involving large amounts of data in that prior can make training expensive. ByPE-VAE replaces the full collection with a small Bayesian pseudocoreset. This compact collection supplies the information used to condition the prior, with the aim of reducing computation and avoiding overfitting.

The pseudocoreset is optimized during VAE training rather than simply selected once and left unchanged. A stochastic optimization procedure seeks to minimize the Kullback-Leibler divergence between the pseudocoreset-based prior and the prior based on the complete dataset. The design therefore gives the smaller prior an explicit target: approximate the distributional behavior of its full-data counterpart.

Experiments report competitive improvements in density estimation, representation learning, and generative data augmentation. On a basic VAE architecture, the method runs up to three times faster than Exemplar VAE while nearly retaining its performance. That result supports the practical value of learning a compact prior representation, with the stated speed comparison tied to that architecture.
neurips-2021-bype-vae-bayesian-pseudocor.tldr: ByPE-VAE learns a small pseudocoreset-based prior to reduce exemplar VAE computation while largely preserving performance.

paragraphs: COHESIV learns to identify the pixels belonging to a hand and the object it holds. Its central source of training information is motion in video. At prediction time, however, the system takes a single RGB image together with the location of a hand, and produces segmentations of the hand and hand-held object.

For training, the method creates responsibility maps that describe how well a hand's movement explains the movement of other pixels. These maps serve as pseudo-labels: automatically generated training targets for a weakly supervised network. The learning objective combines an attention-based similarity loss with a contrastive loss, allowing the network to learn from the motion-derived supervision.

The distinction between training and prediction is central to the approach. Video supplies evidence about the relationship between hands and surrounding pixels, while the trained system can operate on a still image with a supplied hand location. The authors report better performance than alternative methods on 100DOH, EPIC-KITCHENS, and HO3D, supporting the usefulness of this motion-based learning signal.
neurips-2021-cohesiv-contrastive-object-.tldr: COHESIV uses motion-derived training labels to segment hands and held objects from a single image and a hand location.

paragraphs: Computer-aided design relies on highly structured two-dimensional sketches that underpin three-dimensional constructions. Creating these sketches is a demanding part of using CAD software. This paper develops a machine learning model that generates them automatically, with the longer-term aim of supporting tools that reduce the effort engineers spend creating designs.

The method combines a general-purpose language modeling technique with an existing data serialization protocol. Serialization provides a way to express structured sketch data in a form the model can process and generate. This connects the task of producing a CAD sketch with the task of modeling a structured sequence. The authors also explore extensions that give finer control over generation.

The reported results cover both unconditional synthesis and translating images into sketches. The authors find that the approach can accommodate the domain's structural complexity and performs well in both settings. The contribution is a sketch-generation method and a route toward design assistance; the abstract presents broader intelligent engineering tools as a future possibility enabled by this work.
neurips-2021-computer-aided-design-as-la.tldr: The paper combines language modeling and data serialization to generate structured CAD sketches, including sketches derived from images.

paragraphs: Graph embeddings represent nodes with compact vectors while trying to retain useful graph structure. Contrastive learning helps organize those vectors by bringing similar nodes together and separating dissimilar ones. COLES combines this idea with Laplacian Eigenmaps, extending an established approach to representing graph structure in a lower-dimensional space.

The authors examine a contrastive formulation inspired by generative adversarial networks. They show that the Jensen-Shannon divergence used in many contrastive graph models fails when the positive and negative distributions are disjoint, a situation that sampling can produce. Their analysis shows that COLES instead essentially minimizes a surrogate for Wasserstein distance, which can handle distributions with no overlap.

They also place the COLES objective within the family of block-contrastive losses, for which prior work had shown advantages over pairwise losses. On the evaluated benchmarks and backbones, COLES offers favorable accuracy and scalability against several graph-learning baselines. The contribution connects those empirical results to a mathematical explanation of why the contrastive objective remains useful in a problematic sampling regime.
neurips-2021-contrastive-laplacian-eigen.tldr: COLES combines Laplacian Eigenmaps with a contrastive objective designed to handle disjoint positive and negative distributions.

paragraphs: A graph convolutional network typically combines the propagation of features across a graph with nonlinear transformations. Earlier work showed that linear versions can deliver comparable performance with substantially less computation. This paper investigates a remaining difficulty: adding more propagation steps to a linear graph network does not necessarily improve its results.

The authors interpret feature propagation through continuous graph diffusion. This perspective distinguishes the terminal time of diffusion from the number of steps used to carry it out. Their proposed Decoupled Graph Convolution, or DGC, separates those two choices, giving the model more flexibility and allowing it to exploit a very large number of propagation steps.

Experiments show large improvements over the linear graph networks considered and competitive performance against many modern nonlinear variants. The significance is that propagation depth becomes a more useful design choice once it is separated from diffusion duration. The work therefore uses an analysis of the propagation process to improve a computationally efficient class of graph models.
neurips-2021-dissecting-the-diffusion-pr.tldr: DGC improves linear graph networks by separating diffusion duration from the number of feature-propagation steps.

paragraphs: DOCTOR addresses the decision of whether to accept a classifier's prediction or reject it as potentially incorrect. This is useful when a neural network is already trained and may be available only through restricted access. The method aims to detect likely misclassifications so that trust can be assessed separately for each prediction.

The authors study two access settings. In the totally black-box setting, only the model's soft predictions are available. In the partially black-box setting, gradients can also be propagated to support input preprocessing. DOCTOR can be applied to any pretrained model and does not require prior information about the dataset underlying it.

Across the evaluated image and sentiment-analysis datasets, the authors report better empirical performance than the state-of-the-art methods they compare against. In the partially black-box setting, they observe a reduction of up to 4% in false rejection rate. This indicates fewer rejected correct predictions in those experiments, while retaining a method described as comparable in simplicity to the simplest existing approaches.
neurips-2021-doctor-a-simple-method-for-.tldr: DOCTOR assesses whether pretrained classifiers' predictions should be accepted, using either soft predictions alone or additional gradient access.

paragraphs: Natural images contain spatial redundancy, so different regions need not receive the same amount of processing. This paper introduces a Dynamic Grained Encoder that adjusts how many queries a vision transformer assigns to each region. Its aim is to retain detailed representations where they help distinguish image content while reducing computational work elsewhere.

The mechanism uses sparse queries and adapts their allocation across space. Discriminative regions receive a finer representation, allowing the model to devote more of its representational effort to useful details. The encoder is designed to work with most vision transformer frameworks, making the proposed allocation strategy applicable across a broad family of models.

For image classification, the authors report reductions of 40%–60% in computational complexity while maintaining comparable performance with the evaluated state-of-the-art vision transformers. Additional detection and segmentation experiments support the approach's generalizability across vision tasks. These findings concern a more selective use of computation: the encoder changes spatial processing granularity while preserving useful information for the tested tasks.
neurips-2021-dynamic-grained-encoder-for.tldr: The Dynamic Grained Encoder allocates transformer queries by image region, reducing reported classification computation by 40%–60% with comparable performance.

paragraphs: In fixed-confidence pure exploration, a learner samples a stochastic environment to answer a question with a specified level of certainty. The goal is to use as few samples as possible. Lower bounds on the required sampling reveal ideal proportions for drawing different arms, but finding those proportions can itself be computationally demanding.

Frank-Wolfe-based Sampling, or FWS, learns and tracks these proportions through a single iteration of the Frank-Wolfe optimization algorithm applied to the lower-bound problem. This gives the learner an inexpensive way to update its sampling allocation. The method connects the mathematical description of optimal exploration to a practical rule for deciding which observations to collect.

The authors show that FWS matches sample-complexity lower bounds for a wide class of pure-exploration problems. They apply it to tasks including best-arm identification in unstructured, thresholded, linear, and Lipschitz bandits, and report competitive performance against state-of-the-art algorithms. The result combines sampling efficiency with computational simplicity across the studied settings, rather than requiring a complicated allocation procedure.
neurips-2021-fast-pure-exploration-via-f.tldr: FWS uses lightweight Frank-Wolfe updates to achieve sample-efficient exploration with theoretical guarantees across a wide class of bandit problems.

paragraphs: Vision-and-language navigation requires an agent to follow instructions while moving through a visual environment. Choosing the next action can depend on locations and actions far back in its history. HAMT addresses this memory requirement by incorporating a long history of panoramic observations into a transformer-based decision process.

The history encoder operates hierarchically. It first encodes individual images, then models spatial relationships among images within each panorama, and finally models temporal relationships across past panoramas. The action predictor combines this history with the instruction text and current observation. Training starts with end-to-end proxy tasks, including action and spatial-relation prediction, followed by reinforcement learning to improve the navigation policy.

The authors report state-of-the-art results across tasks involving detailed instructions, high-level instructions, dialogue, and long routes. They find the method particularly effective when trajectories are longer. These results support the usefulness of explicitly organizing visual memory at several scales, so that information from earlier observations can participate in the current navigation decision.
neurips-2021-history-aware-multimodal-tr.tldr: HAMT combines hierarchically encoded visual history with instructions and current observations to improve navigation, especially on longer routes.

paragraphs: Neural compression methods can achieve strong compression ratios, but their processing speed can hinder practical use. iFlow addresses this problem for lossless compression based on normalizing flows. Its objective is to preserve the compression advantages of these generative models while making the coding process substantially faster.

The method has two main components. First, the authors introduce the Modular Scale Transform and use it to construct a family of numerically invertible flow transformations. Numerical invertibility matters to lossless compression because decoding must recover the original data exactly. Second, they introduce the Uniform Base Conversion System, a fast codec for uniform distributions that becomes part of the iFlow compression framework.

The paper reports state-of-the-art compression ratios together with coding that is five times faster than other high-performance schemes. It also states that its techniques can accelerate a broad class of flow-based algorithms. The contribution therefore spans both the transformations used by the model and the coding machinery needed to turn those transformations into efficient compression.
neurips-2021-iflow-numerically-invertibl.tldr: iFlow combines numerically invertible transformations with a fast uniform codec to deliver efficient lossless neural compression.

paragraphs: Forecasting a physical system beyond observed data benefits from a model that respects its governing structure. Prior approaches imposed Hamiltonian or Lagrangian forms suited to reversible dynamics. This paper develops a structure-preserving approach for irreversible processes, where dissipation must be represented even when the model's functional form is not known beforehand.

The authors introduce a parameterization of dissipative brackets within metriplectic dynamical systems. The learned structure includes generalized Casimirs associated with energy and entropy, guaranteeing energy conservation and nondecreasing entropy, respectively. These properties are built into the representation of the dynamics, so learning operates within a form that already enforces the stated physical behavior.

When thermal noise is added, the method also guarantees exact preservation of a fluctuation-dissipation theorem, maintaining thermodynamic consistency in that setting. Benchmarks on dissipative systems show greater robustness and better generalization than black-box or penalty-based approaches. The findings support using structural constraints as part of the model itself when forecasting irreversible dynamics from time-series data.
neurips-2021-machine-learning-structure-.tldr: The paper learns irreversible dynamics using a structure that guarantees energy conservation, nondecreasing entropy, and thermodynamic consistency under added thermal noise.

paragraphs: A two-sample test asks whether two collections of observations come from different distributions. Kernel-based methods can distinguish complex, high-dimensional distributions by learning a suitable comparison function. When only a few observations are available, however, learning that function directly can be difficult. This paper investigates how experience from related testing problems can help.

The proposed meta two-sample testing problem assumes abundant auxiliary data from related tasks. The aim is to learn an algorithm that can quickly identify a powerful test for a new target task with little data. The authors develop two approaches: a generic meta-testing scheme and a more tailored method that performs better in their evaluations.

The paper provides theoretical justification and empirical evidence that these schemes outperform learning kernel tests directly from scarce target observations. It also identifies conditions under which meta-testing succeeds. The central benefit is the transfer of useful testing experience across related tasks, making limited target data more informative when appropriate auxiliary data is available.
neurips-2021-meta-two-sample-testing-lea.tldr: Meta two-sample testing uses data from related tasks to learn stronger distribution-comparison tests when target observations are scarce.

paragraphs: The Fisher information matrix is used to study neural-network loss landscapes, support second-order optimization, and describe learning geometrically. Computing it exactly is often impractical or impossible in closed form, so applications generally estimate it from samples. This paper examines how much uncertainty those sample-based estimates introduce.

The authors study two estimators derived from mathematically equivalent representations of the Fisher information matrix. Both are unbiased and consistent: they target the correct matrix in expectation and converge appropriately as sampling increases. Those properties do not by themselves describe how much an estimate fluctuates with finite data. The paper derives closed-form variance expressions to characterize that aspect of estimation quality.

The analysis investigates how a deep network's parameter structure affects estimator variance and discusses upper bounds on that variance. This connects the reliability of a Fisher estimate to the model being analyzed. The contribution provides tools for assessing estimation quality when Fisher information is used in deep learning, beyond simply knowing that an estimator has the correct long-run target.
neurips-2021-on-the-variance-of-the-fish.tldr: The paper derives and analyzes the variance of two Fisher information estimators to clarify their reliability for deep neural networks.

paragraphs: UMAP is widely used to visualize high-dimensional data, but its effective optimization behavior is not fully explained by its published objective. This paper analyzes the sampling procedure used during optimization and derives the loss function that the procedure actually implements. The resulting expression differs from the published loss in a way that depends on dataset size.

That difference changes the interpretation of what UMAP seeks to preserve. The authors show that it does not aim to reproduce the theoretically motivated high-dimensional similarities usually associated with the method. Instead, its effective targets encode the nearest-neighbor graph. The analysis therefore shifts attention from those original similarity values to the neighborhood relationships represented by that graph.

The authors suggest that negative sampling's implicit balance between attraction and repulsion is key to UMAP's success. They support their theoretical findings with experiments on toy data and single-cell RNA sequencing data. The work offers a revised explanation of the algorithm's behavior, while presenting the importance of that balance as their interpretation of its effectiveness.
neurips-2021-on-umap-s-true-loss-functio.tldr: The paper derives UMAP's effective loss and shows that its sampling procedure changes which high-dimensional relationships it aims to preserve.

paragraphs: Differential-equation models are often fitted to numerical measurements collected over time. Sometimes the available evidence instead records qualitative changes as a controlled condition varies. These changes are bifurcations, and their arrangement forms a bifurcation diagram. This paper proposes learning model parameters directly from a user-specified diagram.

The approach uses a cost function with two complementary parts. One measures agreement between the model's bifurcations and the target change points. The other supplies gradients that steer optimization toward parameter regions where bifurcations occur. This helps address both finding the relevant kind of behavior and placing its changes appropriately. The gradients can be computed without differentiating through the solver operations used to obtain the diagram.

The authors demonstrate inference on minimal models involving saddle-node and pitchfork diagrams, as well as a genetic toggle switch from synthetic biology. They also show that the cost landscape can organize models by topological and geometric equivalence. The method thus treats qualitative changes as useful fitting evidence and provides a way to compare the resulting model behaviors.
neurips-2021-parameter-inference-with-bi.tldr: The paper fits differential-equation parameters to target bifurcation diagrams using gradients that do not require differentiating through the diagram solver.

paragraphs: PALMS studies how to adjust a language model's behavior toward a predetermined set of values. The motivation is that generated language can be harmful, biased, or undesirable within a particular cultural context. The proposed process uses a small, manually curated dataset whose examples reflect the chosen behavioral targets.

The process alternates fine-tuning with evaluation. Human judgments assess whether outputs follow the target values, toxicity scoring measures another aspect of output behavior, and qualitative analysis examines words commonly associated with social categories. Shortcomings found through these evaluations guide the addition of further training examples. The dataset therefore develops in response to observed model behavior.

Across a broad range of GPT-3 model sizes, PALMS performs significantly better than baseline and control models on all reported evaluation measures without compromising capability integrity. Its effectiveness increases with model size in the reported study. These findings show that a small curated dataset can substantially change behavior toward specified values; the targets remain those selected for the process and its cultural context.
neurips-2021-process-for-adapting-langua.tldr: PALMS iteratively curates fine-tuning examples to move language-model behavior toward specified values, with stronger reported effects in larger models.

paragraphs: Plug-and-play priors and regularization by denoising use pretrained denoising networks to help solve inverse imaging problems. Their empirical performance and convergence behavior had already received substantial attention. This paper focuses on a different question: what can theoretically be said about the quality of the recovered solution, beyond whether an algorithm converges?

The authors establish a route to recovery guarantees by assuming that the methods' solution lies near fixed points of a deep neural network. A fixed point is an input that the network leaves unchanged. This assumption links the recovered solution to the network's behavior and supports the theoretical recovery analysis. The guarantees therefore depend on a stated relationship between the solution and those fixed points.

The paper also evaluates recovery in compressive sensing against recent methods based on generative models. Its numerical results suggest that plug-and-play reconstruction with a pretrained artifact-removal network gives significantly better results than the compared state-of-the-art methods. The work combines conditional theoretical guarantees with empirical evidence about a specific reconstruction setting.
neurips-2021-recovery-analysis-for-plug-.tldr: The paper establishes conditional recovery guarantees for denoiser-based inverse methods and reports promising compressive-sensing results.

paragraphs: Many graph-neural-network explanations identify a subgraph that is strongly associated with a prediction. The paper argues that optimizing this association for one input can fit noise, and that removing the highlighted subgraph need not change the prediction. It seeks explanations that are both resistant to noise and counterfactual in their effect on the model.

The proposed method models decision logic shared across similar input graphs. Its explanations draw on common decision boundaries governing many predictions, rather than an independently optimized correlation for one graph. Each explanation identifies edges whose removal significantly changes the prediction. This connects the highlighted graph structure to a concrete intervention on the model's input.

The authors attribute the explanations' noise robustness to their grounding in shared decision boundaries. They report superior performance through extensive experiments on public datasets. The contribution brings together two goals: identifying a meaningful change to a particular prediction and using behavior across similar graphs to avoid explanations driven by noise in that single example.
neurips-2021-robust-counterfactual-expla.tldr: The method explains graph-network predictions through edge removals derived from decision logic shared across similar graphs.

paragraphs: Thompson sampling with Gaussian-process models is a useful approach to optimizing functions whose internal form is unknown. Its computational overhead grows polynomially with the evaluation budget, making long optimization runs costly. Sparse Gaussian-process approximations offer a more scalable alternative for problems requiring many evaluations, including noisy, multimodal, or combinatorial tasks.

The difficulty is that introducing an approximation changes the basis for existing theoretical guarantees. Earlier regret bounds no longer apply directly to sparse models. This paper supplies a theoretical and empirical analysis of scalable Thompson sampling, establishing guarantees that account for the approximation rather than assuming the standard analysis remains valid.

The authors show that the substantial reduction in computation can be obtained without losing the regret performance of standard Thompson sampling. They support these claims with practical implementations on synthetic benchmarks and a high-throughput molecular-design task. The contribution gives theoretical backing to scalable variants and checks that the anticipated computational and optimization benefits appear in the evaluated applications.
neurips-2021-scalable-thompson-sampling-.tldr: The paper provides theoretical and empirical support for sparse-GP Thompson sampling that reduces computation without losing standard Thompson sampling's regret performance.

paragraphs: Non-rigid shape registration aligns three-dimensional point clouds even when the shapes deform. This paper proposes a data-driven transformer procedure for that task. It supports registering acquired geometry to a fixed template, allowing template properties such as animation cues to transfer to the input, and registering one shape directly to another.

In the second setting, the method produces dense correspondences between shapes. These matches support applications including texture transfer and shape interpolation. The authors also find that estimating the underlying surface density makes learning easier. Their model can be trained with ground-truth correspondences for only about 10%–20% of the total points, reducing the amount of correspondence supervision required.

Qualitative and quantitative evaluations report better performance than state-of-the-art methods across different datasets and registration scenarios. The findings show how a transformer architecture can support matching deformable, unordered geometric data. They also connect the learned correspondences to practical uses: transferring properties from a template or establishing relationships between two independently supplied shapes.
neurips-2021-shape-registration-in-the-t.tldr: The paper uses transformers to register deformable 3D point clouds and learn dense matches with sparse correspondence supervision.

paragraphs: Two neural networks can share an architecture yet develop different internal activations because training starts from different initializations. This paper asks how closely those representations can be matched. Its Dr. Frankenstein toolset connects selected layers of two trained networks using a stitching layer that maps between their activations.

The authors investigate several classes of linear transformations for this connecting layer and examine their properties and performance. They demonstrate that representations in deep convolutional networks with the same architecture can be matched with surprisingly high accuracy, even using a single affine transformation. This makes the complexity of the required alignment part of the investigation.

The stitching approach also offers a task-based perspective on representation similarity. Instead of interpreting similarity solely through a numerical index, it examines how a connection between representations performs on a task. The findings show substantial matchability in the studied networks and provide a complementary way to evaluate whether differences in internal activations correspond to meaningful functional differences.
neurips-2021-similarity-and-matching-of-.tldr: The paper shows that a simple stitching layer can closely match representations across differently initialized convolutional networks with the same architecture.

paragraphs: Online optimization makes decisions over successive rounds while accumulating regret relative to a comparison choice. This paper studies Online Lazy Gradient Descent when the feasible domain is strongly convex. The central question is whether the same algorithm can offer strong guarantees both against adversarial opponents and when opponents are independent and identically distributed.

The algorithm was already known to achieve regret of order √N in the adversarial setting. The authors establish expected regret of order log N in the independent, identically distributed setting. This is the sense in which they call it universal: one algorithm achieves both rates under their respective assumptions. The result improves the adversarial rate of a more complex earlier meta-algorithm while retaining its logarithmic stochastic rate.

The paper also shows that order bounds for pseudo-regret and expected regret are equivalent on strongly convex domains, unlike on the simplex. Both contributions emphasize the role of the feasible set's geometry. The stated universality and the equivalence of regret bounds are tied to that domain condition.
neurips-2021-the-lazy-online-subgradient.tldr: On strongly convex domains, Online Lazy Gradient Descent achieves √N adversarial regret and logarithmic expected regret against i.i.d. opponents.

paragraphs: Instance-discriminative self-supervised learning builds representations without supervised labels and often uses many negative samples. Empirically, adding negatives can improve later classification, even when their number exceeds the number of supervised classes. Existing theoretical analysis had instead predicted that large numbers of negatives would degrade downstream classification performance.

This paper develops a different analytical framework using the coupon collector's problem, which concerns how repeated sampling accumulates coverage of categories. Within this framework, increasing the number of negative samples allows the authors' bound to implicitly incorporate the downstream supervised loss into the self-supervised loss. The analysis creates a connection between the training objective and the classification task that follows.

The authors confirm their proposed analysis on real-world benchmark datasets. Its significance is explanatory: it addresses the disagreement between earlier theoretical predictions and observed benefits from additional negatives. The result supplies a framework for understanding those benefits through the relationship between self-supervised training and downstream supervised loss, rather than establishing that more negatives must improve every possible setting.
neurips-2021-understanding-negative-samp.tldr: A coupon-collector-based analysis helps explain why more negative samples can improve downstream classification in self-supervised representation learning.
